zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-checks used the supplied Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, licensed CC BY 4.0 (release: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The scan-grounded readings and English review notes are this review's own work, not a replacement NINJAL transcription.

lines.note: Namecuji is the slug-name; the Portuguese gives only 'a creature so called'. No narrower zoological identification is supplied in the transcription.
Namecujiri is the Cami regional equivalent of the preceding slug-name. Idem carries that definition forward; Cami occurs within the Portuguese usage explanation.
Nameracana describes something smooth and slippery. The Portuguese pair liſa and eſcorregadia supports the adjective rather than a separate object-name.
Nameracani is the corresponding adverb, 'smoothly'; Adu. is the printed grammatical label. Its meaning is inherited from the preceding adjective, not omitted running text.
Nameracaſa is the nominal formation 'smoothness'. The scan places it on its own indented row without a Portuguese gloss, and that physical arrangement is retained.
This regional verb means 'to slip'. The printed principal parts u and etta are preserved rather than regularized; upright X. is the regional label, followed by a comparison with Cami usage.

runs.text: ſe diz Suberu. ¶ Item, Ser a couſa eſcor-

lines.note: Cami usage calls the action Suberu. A second sense then describes a thing as slippery; eſcor- continues into regadia on the next row. Suberu is a Japanese word embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Completes eſcorregadia, 'slippery', in the second sense of Nameri. This short continuation is a full physical text row, not furniture.
Namexi and Namexigaua denote tanned hide or leather. The alternative marker l is preserved, as is the historical Portuguese spelling cortida.
This mushroom-name is glossed by Cugumelos. The scan supports the sequence zuſuqi; the unfamiliar Japanese form is not replaced by a modern mushroom-name.
Nami means waves. Namiga xizzumaru begins the first example, 'the waves subside', whose Portuguese translation follows on the next row.
The opening translates the subsiding of waves. Namini voboruru then gives 'drown in the waves', with initial v retained in the historical spelling of the verb.
The Portuguese completes the drowning example. Namiga voco- starts the next example about waves rising, with the verb divided at the printed hyphen.
Voco- plus ru and the alternative tatçu both describe waves rising. Na- begins the following Namiga example and is not an independent word.
Na- plus miga vtçu means 'the waves strike'. The citation begins Iſo v-, continued as vtçu on the next physical line; no extra punctuation is supplied after ondas.

runs.text: tçu namino qixini atatte cayeruga goto-

lines.note: Continues the comparison with waves striking the shore and returning. The printed qixini and cayeruga identify the shore and the returning action; goto- is completed below.
Goto- plus cu closes the comparison. The source label is Taif.; enlargement clearly gives book 16, not the OCR's 10. Como on- starts the Portuguese translation, 'like waves'.

runs.text: das que batem na praya dando na rocha tornão.

lines.note: Completes ondas and the comparison: waves strike the shore and return after hitting the rock. This is the conclusion of the citation, not another Nami entry.
This separate Nami entry concerns being in common or among others, rather than water-waves. The comma introduces the continuation and examples below.
Sônamini illustrates the collective or ordinary manner, 'in common, or like'. Both nasal abbreviations in cõmũ are retained without expansion.
Os outros completes 'like the others'. Namifazzureno fitogia then describes a person outside the ordinary run, with the historical fazzure spelling retained.

runs.text: Homem que não he dos ordinarios.

lines.note: Translates the preceding example as a man who is not one of the ordinary people. It explains exceptional status without specifying whether that distinction is good or bad.
Namida means tears. The first example begins 'tears in the sleeve'; ſode- is a visibly divided word, not the end of the Japanese sentence.
Completes Namidauo ſodeni tçutçumu, literally wrapping tears in a sleeve and glossed 'to weep'. A new example beginning Namidani continues below.

Namidani mǔſuru and the alternative muxebu describe choking or sobbing with tears, glossed 'weep greatly'. Ink obscures the first vowel of mǔſuru; the OCR's caron is retained provisionally, not treated as secure evidence of vowel length.
Restores the visible initial paragraph sign. Namidani xizzumu, 'sink in tears', receives the same weeping gloss; the following Nami- begins the next example.
Completes Namidauo coboſu, with nagaſu as an alternative: shedding or letting tears flow. Mui- begins muitas in the Portuguese continuation.
Completes 'shed many tears'. Namidagumu introduces eyes filling with tears; the Portuguese verb Arra- continues on the following row.
Completes Arraſaremſe, describing the eyes brimming with tears. The next Namida- is physically divided before its attached object particle.

runs.text: Virem as lagrimas a os olhos.

lines.note: Completes Namidauo moyouoſu, bringing tears to the eyes. The scan's separated a os is retained rather than contracted to modern aos.
Voſayuru and todomuru give two ways of holding back tears. The romanized Japanese example occupies the whole row after the paragraph sign; its translation follows below.
Translates the preceding restraint of tears. The next verb begins vo-; the right-edge mark is a hyphen, not the OCR's full stop, and joins xinogô below.
Vo- plus xinogô is glossed as wiping away tears. The printed final circumflex is preserved; Na- begins the following Namida example, not a separate interjection.
Completes Namida xeqiayezu, inability to hold tears back. Historical xe supplies the expected se-series sound; la- starts lagrimas across the line break.
Completes lagrimas, then introduces Namidani cururu, eyes becoming dark or clouded with tears. Eſcure- is the beginning of the Portuguese verb below.

runs.text: cerem ſe os olhos com lagrimas. ¶

lines.note: Finishes the description of eyes darkened by tears. The next Nami- introduces a characterization of a person's readiness to weep.

Completes Namida mǒroi fito, a person quick to tears. The faint mark over the first o of mǒroi is retained as the provisional caron from the aligned draft; its precise shape is less secure than the word's identification.
Restores the initial paragraph sign and introduces the contrasting person who is resistant to tears. Namidagatai and namidazzuyoi are alternatives; the printed double z is retained.

Describes a dry-eyed person who finds it difficult to weep, translating the preceding contrast. Enlargement supports dificil, with the fi combination followed by cil, rather than the truncated OCR difil; no second f is supplied.
Namidagaua, literally a river of tears, is marked P. for poetic use and glossed as abundance or a torrent. The label is upright in the scan, unlike the following italic definition.
Completes 'an abundance or torrent of tears'. The short row belongs to Namidagaua and is not a separate dictionary entry.
Namidagumi gives the principal forms of the verb for eyes filling with tears. The historical abbreviated u and unda are retained, and o- begins olhos below.

runs.text: lhos em lagrimas, ou ter os olhos choroſos, ou

lines.note: Completes olhos and offers the alternative description 'have tearful eyes'. The final ou introduces one more paraphrase on the next row.
Completes the appearance-based gloss: eyes like those of someone about to cry. It does not assert that tears have already been shed.
Namigi denotes a sea route. The repeated form begins an example whose attached object particle and verb follow on the next row.
Completes Namigiuo xinogu, enduring the hardships of a sea passage. The gloss's Paßar is retained with its printed doubled-s sort rather than modernized.

Nami j, iru, ita concerns sitting or being together in an ordered row. The second pass preserves the clearly wider gap before j instead of the joined OCR Namij. A visible word space restores Estarem todos; or- continues as ordem at the top of the second column.

Completes ordem from the preceding column: everyone occupies their places in order. The example begins with the eight people just mentioned and na-, continued below. The row is visibly indented like the following continuation lines.
Na- plus miite describes the people seated together; vomoizaxi and vomoidori concern passing and taking the cup at will. Jixacu ji- begins the self-serving arrangement continued on the next row.
Completes jimorino and describes a convivial amusement, drinking while dancing and singing. The historical mǒtçu and vtǒtçu forms are retained exactly rather than replaced with modern conjugations.

runs.text: Eſtando oito peßoas juntas fizerão hum

lines.note: Tac. is the upright citation label. The Portuguese starts the translation: eight people gathered together held a drinking party, completed on the next row.

runs.text: beberete em q̃ hum mandaua o Sacazzuqui a-

lines.note: The party involved each person sending the drinking cup to whomever he wished. The scan's Sacazzuqui is retained, including its unusual qui sequence; it is a Japanese noun embedded in Portuguese. The abbreviation q̃ remains unexpanded.

runs.text: quem queria, & tomaua de quem queria, tomã-

lines.note: Completes a quem queria and adds taking the cup from whomever one wished. Tomã- begins tomando across the physical break, with the printed nasal abbreviation retained.

runs.text: do cada hum por ſi officio de eſcanção, ora bai

lines.note: Each person acts as his own cupbearer. The closing bai continues into bailauão below, but no hyphen is visible at this line's right edge, so none is invented.
Completes bailauão and ends the party description: they alternately danced and sang while drinking. The final-a tilde in cantauã is preserved rather than expanded.
Namima is the space or interval between waves. Upright S. marks written usage and is separate from the italic definition.
Namimacura, a wave-pillow expression, refers poetically to sleeping aboard ship. P. is an upright poetic-use label; the alternative wording continues below.
Completes the poetic gloss as sleeping 'upon the waves'. It is the continuation of Namimacura, not an independent literal object-name.
Namiſuye means setting people or things in order or in a row. The two consecutive Portuguese forms Por por serve different grammatical functions and are not a duplicated OCR word.
Fileira completes 'in a row', the second description of arranging things in order. The standalone word remains on its own physical line.

runs.text: Borda do mar, ou praya on-

lines.note: Namiuchiguiua denotes the water's edge or shore where waves strike. On- begins the relative word onde, not another Japanese component.
Completes onde batem as ondas, locating the shore at the place where waves break. This finishes the preceding compound's definition.
Namiyori is glossed as waves becoming ruffled. Its printed principal parts are preserved; the following figurative extension applies the wrinkling image to other materials.
The figurative extension is wrinkling or puckering a thing. Permet. remains an unexpanded printed label, and cou- continues into couſa below.
Completes couſa and gives cloth and a mat as examples of wrinkling. The scan supplies eſteira, not the OCR's eſtira; the historical spelling and compressed punctuation are otherwise retained.
Namomi is a plant-name glossed simply as 'a herb so called'. The text does not supply enough botanical detail to insert a species identification.

runs.text: Palaura com que ſe inuoca, ou faz re-

lines.note: Namu is explained as a formula of invocation or reverence. Inuoca restores the visible historical u/v spelling, rather than OCR innoca; re- continues as reuerencia below.
Completes reverence to Fotoque and gives Namu Amidabut as an example. Fotoque is embedded in Portuguese; Amidabut belongs to the separate Japanese invocation and retains its final checked t.

Gives the second invocation, referring to the Lotus teaching. The supplied long-vowel signs are retained; the mark after f is faint but compatible with the provisional caron, not grounds for normalizing the whole phrase. The row is indented in the scan like the preceding continuation, and its placement has been corrected.

runs.text: Palaura com que os gentios inuo-

lines.note: Namuſanbô is an invocation of the Three Jewels. The Portuguese begins its explanation in the missionary dictionary's own terminology; inuo- continues on the next physical row.

runs.text: caõ o Fotoque, os bonzos, & liuro da ley como

lines.note: Completes inuocaõ and lists Fotoque, the monks, and the book of the teaching. This is the source's formulation of the three sacred objects; its wording is preserved rather than doctrinally rewritten.
Completes the gloss as 'three sacred things'. The short line closes the Namuſanbô explanation and does not belong to the following Nan entry.
Nan is paired with Catai and glossed as danger or difficulty. Nannivǒ illustrates encountering adversity; the joined Japanese spacing and the printed caron are retained.
Completes Encontrar, 'encounter difficulties'. It translates the preceding Nannivǒ example, rather than introducing a new meaning independently.
This Nan means a defect or fault. Nanuo yǔ gives the related act of expressing criticism or finding fault, distinguished from danger in the preceding entry.
Translates the example as criticizing or disparaging someone. The printed deſdanhar is preserved, not regularized to a modern Portuguese form.
A third Nan is the male/man sense, explained by Vonoco and Portuguese Varão. Vonoco is a Japanese synonym, not a term embedded in a Portuguese sentence.

runs.text: Madronhado que ſe faz no metal,

lines.note: Nanaco is a textured ornamental finish applied to metal. The definition's Madronhado describes the surface pattern; the examples of objects bearing it continue below.

runs.text: nos cabos das Catanas, nos relicarios, &c.

lines.note: Names sword hilts and reliquaries as places where the metal ornament occurs. The capitalization of Catanas is preserved as printed within the Portuguese explanation.

Nanacuſa is explained as seven herbs used at the New Year. The scan gives the intact Japanese term Xǒguachi within the italic Portuguese explanation, not the OCR's split Xògua chi; no full stop is supplied after no.

runs.text: as quais machocadas cozem com Miſò, & co-

lines.note: The herbs are crushed and cooked with Miſò. That Japanese ingredient-name is embedded in Portuguese and keeps its printed grave accent; co- continues as comem below.

runs.text: mem por feſta do anno nouo.

lines.note: Completes comem and explains that the preparation is eaten for the New Year celebration. The line closes the seven-herb entry without adding a date absent from the source.
Naname and Nanamena describe something slanting, crooked, or curved. Ar- is the first part of arcada in the Portuguese explanation, not a new Japanese form.
Completes arcada and gives Nijiga nanamena, referring to the rainbow's curved shape. O arco begins its Portuguese translation on this row.
The rainbow is said not to be straight. Figa nana- begins the second example, now concerning the sun's inclination rather than the rainbow's curve.

runs.text: Està o ſol inclinado pera a parte

lines.note: Completes Figa nanamena, 'the sun is inclined'. The printed grave in Està and the historical pera are retained; the direction is supplied below.
Completes the setting-sun example as inclination toward the west. Upright S. is the written-usage label, not part of the italic Portuguese sentence.
Nanameni is the corresponding adverb, 'obliquely' or 'at a slant'. Aduer. is the printed grammatical abbreviation and inherits its lexical meaning from the preceding entry.

Nanban is explained by Minamino yebiſu and glossed as the southern regions. The Japanese synonym and the Portuguese geographical gloss are retained without imposing a narrower modern national reference.
Nanbangocu is the example for kingdoms in the southern regions. Vt is italic in the scan; the Japanese example remains upright between it and the Portuguese translation.
Nanbanmono denotes something from the southern regions. This compound extends the geographical sense of Nanban, not the following difficulty-related Nanbiǒ.
Nanbiǒ is a dangerous or difficult illness, explained by Catai yamai. The caron over o is visible and belongs to this headword's own spelling.
Nanbǒ denotes the southern direction, literally Minamino cata. The scan clearly reads do ſul, correcting the OCR's co ſul; the caron distinguishes this printed headword from the next one.
Nanbô asks how many or how much there is. Its circumflex is distinct from the preceding caron, and the question mark belongs to the italic Portuguese gloss.
